doc.title: Annie Ross interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001

title: First club job in London
summary: At 17 she joined her family in Scotland, then took a London club job for seven pounds ten a week, singing standards with a band.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Well I’m in the process of doing that now.
Great. And so you say your family went back to Europe and you followed?
Back to Scotland. No I didn’t see them until I was 17.
And then I stayed a couple of weeks and went down to London. I got a job in a club, bought a second-hand dress and I thought I’d died and gone to heaven.
Can you recall what kind of wages you were working for back then?
Oh yes, seven pound ten a week.

About ten bucks a week. But I didn’t care. It was enough to pay my rent. I could eat at the club, I was singing many obscure Rogers & Hart and Cole Porter and Jerome Kern. I mean they had never heard that before. It was a private club, very snooty. But they did give me a little button to switch on when I got up to sing, which gave me a little spotlight. A bit like Marilyn Monroe in “Bus Stop.”
Yeah. Was that — is the word “cabaret singer” appropriate here?
A cabaret singer gives a performance. I didn’t give a performance, I sang with a band, which was as it should be. I was starting out, it was the best experience.
And again, what kind of tunes would that particular band have been doing?
Oh, “I’ve Got Five Dollars,” and you know, all the great standards of the time.
